methodology: Synthetic event vectors are replayed against the unmodified engine under a virtual clock with a seeded RNG (mulberry32), making every run deterministic and reproducible on any machine. No network access is required.

vectors.description: 90 s of organic desktop interaction — log-normal inter-event timing (median 220 ms), curved pointer paths with angular wobble, ~6% keystroke corrections, irregular scroll velocities with direction changes.
60 s of organic mobile interaction — touch contact-area variance, swipe character, live gyroscope micro-motion around 9.78 m/s².

120 s of canonical scripted-bot input — perfectly uniform 100 ms cadence, deterministic round-robin event types, constant-velocity straight-line movement, constant scroll speed, fixed tap coordinates, zero corrections.
120 s of randomized scripted input — uniform-random 80–160 ms cadence, straight-line constant-step pointer movement, no long pauses. Tests the synthetic-cadence anomaly detection (pause tail).

INFORMATIONAL (open limitation): 120 s of adaptive mimicry — log-normal timing, organic curves, corrections, scroll direction changes, variable-duration touches. Mirrors the human generator one-to-one; documents the statistical detection boundary. Not counted in the pass/fail summary.

notes: bot_uniform encodes the documented bot signatures: uniform timing, straight-line movement, constant velocity, fixed coordinates, no corrections.
bot_jitter is the cheap-evasion class: randomized timing without a human pause tail. Caught by the synthetic-cadence anomaly checks (no long intervals, compressed tail).

bot_mimic is published INFORMATIONALLY: it mirrors the human generator's statistics one-to-one and currently verifies as human (see test-results.json). No statistical sensor can separate perfect mimicry from its own synthetic human baseline — defeating this class requires challenge-response or hardware signals (v1.1, ROADMAP.md). Published to document the boundary honestly.

What PASS proves: the engine classifies the published patterns into the published expected ranges, deterministically, on any machine. It does not prove field accuracy against unknown adaptive attackers.
